items.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006
items.q: I mean can you imagine if when Ravel wrote Bolero that he was still thinking about sixteenth century harmony and treatises and terms, you know, parallel fourths and fifths?

ctx.x: You never can have enough. You never can have enough because as you discover certain things harmonically that can happen and melodically — see to me rhythm, melody and harmony are one. They are not separate. You know we teach them separately but they’re really one movement together. They function as one. When you start to break them down into the different boxes that’s when you start to lose it. Because there are certain things that might be happening melodically that has nothing to do with the harmony and…
That’s right. Ooh I can’t write that.
